text: You get an integer array called hand, and an integer called group size. Return true if you can split all the cards into groups. Each group has exactly group-size cards, and the values in a group are consecutive.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — every card must be used, and each card goes into exactly one group. A group like two, three, four is fine, but two, two, three is not. And the order of the cards in the hand doesn't matter, because I can rearrange them. Is that right?
Yes. All cards used, no repeats inside a group, and order doesn't matter.

Okay. Then only two things matter: which values I have, and how many copies of each. So I can think in counts, not in positions. And here's the key fact I want to plant early. Look at the smallest card that's left. It can't be in the middle of a group, because nothing smaller is left to come before it. So it must start a group. And if it has several copies — say count copies — every one of those copies must start its own group. Are there any constraints on the input size?
The hand has between one and ten to the fourth cards. Each card value is between zero and ten to the ninth. And group size is at least one, and at most the length of the hand.

Got it. Values go up to ten to the ninth, so I can't index an array by value — I'll need a map, and I'll keep overflow in mind for k plus i. Let me run through the example. One, two, three, six, two, three, four, seven, eight, with a group size of three. The smallest card always starts the next group, so I get one, two, three, then two, three, four, then six, seven, eight. Everything's used, so the answer is true. The second example, one through five with size four: one, two, three, four is a group, and five is left alone with no six. So false.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to backtrack — try every way to build each group, and undo when I get stuck. That's exponential, and with ten thousand cards it won't finish. This problem reminds me of a greedy pass over a sorted count map. The fact from before removes all the choice: the smallest card has only one legal role, so there's nothing to try. And I don't build one group at a time. If the smallest value k has count copies, I start that many groups at once, so I subtract count from each of k through k plus group size minus one in a single pass. I'll go with an ordered map from int to int — it gives me the counts, and sorted keys for free.

Here's the plan. The state is a frequency map of unused copies, and the invariant is: when I reach key k, every smaller key is already zero. First, build the map from the hand. Second, walk the keys in increasing order; copy the count — not a reference — and skip the key if it's zero. Third, for each of the next group-size values, return false if it's missing or short; otherwise subtract count. If all pass, return true. One thing worth flagging — the invariant makes the greedy safe. The copies of k can't join an earlier group, so they must start new ones, and a short value has no other placement. So failing right away is correct, not just fast. A sort plus a hash map also works; the ordered map is shorter. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. One loop builds the map. A second loop walks it with a structured binding, k and v: I copy v into count, skip zeros, and the inner loop checks and subtracts at k plus i. That matches the plan line by line. One thing worth flagging — copying v into count is needed for correctness. v is a reference to the entry for k, and at i equals zero the subtraction sets that entry to zero. If I used v directly, every later check would use zero, and the groups would never really be taken out. The zero skip matters too: used-up keys stay in the map, and starting groups at them could wrongly return false.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. Example one, group size three, expected true. The key row is key two. It started with two copies, but the group at one already used one, so count is one and I start only one group: two, three, four. That's the invariant at work — key one is already zero. The rest is skips plus six, seven, eight, so true. The case where the copy earns its place is one, one, two, two, three, three, three, four, five, size three: at key one, count is two, so two groups start at once, and it returns true. Corner cases: group size one is always true. Five, five, five with size three is false. And the largest k plus i ever computed is ten to the ninth plus one, well below int max.

Let me think about complexity here. The nested loop looks like n times g, but it isn't. Every passing inner step subtracts at least one card, so across the whole run the inner loop takes at most n plus one steps — at ten thousand cards, the most I saw was ten thousand and one. The time complexity is n log n, dominated by building the map. The space complexity is linear, one entry per distinct value. In the worst case, all values are distinct, and it still runs in about three milliseconds. Against exhaustive backtracking on two hundred seventy thousand, five hundred ninety-two cases, there were zero mismatches. Oh, one more thing — I don't check up front whether the hand size divides by group size. It's still correct without it, but that one-line check is a cheap, optional early exit.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You planted the greedy fact early: the smallest card must start a group, so you start all of those groups at once. You explained why the count has to be a copy, since v becomes zero the moment you subtract at i equals zero — and why the zero-skip is needed. And you showed the nested loop is really n plus one steps in total, not n times g. Good work.
